issues.description: The Discussion section states the meta-analytic effect size for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' was 'significantly different from zero,' but the Results section reports p = .065 for this same analysis. At the conventional α = .05 threshold, p = .065 is not statistically significant. This represents a direct factual error that inflates the apparent evidentiary support for an effect that the Results section correctly characterizes as non-significant.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero. We believe that it will be unlikely that future studies will find an effect similar to the original, supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.

issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the CREP minimum sample size for this replication was set at 120 participants 'to ensure adequate statistical power,' and claims all studies in the meta-analysis collected this minimum. However, Table 1 shows the Gordon College study had N = 80, which is 33% below the stated minimum and equal to the original study's sample size. This undermines the claim of adequate power and raises questions about why this study was included despite failing to meet pre-specified inclusion criteria.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power), posted their raw dataset, and reported a summary of results.

issues.description: The fail-safe N (FSN) for the 'Opportunity to Express Self' meta-analysis is reported as 3 in the Results section, but is then described as 5 in the Discussion section. These are direct numerical contradictions within the same manuscript for the same statistic from the same analysis. The FSN is used to draw substantive interpretive conclusions about effect stability, so this inconsistency directly affects the validity of those conclusions.
issues.quote: Results: 'The FSN was 3 studies.' Discussion: 'The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.'

issues.description: The fail-safe N for the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' meta-analysis is reported as 5 in the Results section, but is then stated as 11 in the Discussion section. These values differ by more than twofold and are used to reach conclusions about the stability of the meta-analytic results. This is a second independent FSN reporting inconsistency in the same manuscript.
issues.quote: Results: 'The FSN was 5 studies.' Discussion: 'These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).'

issues.description: The original study's effect size for 'Self-Disclosure Advantages' is reported as -.30 in both the Abstract and Table 1 (as β), but as -.33 in Table 3 and in the Discussion section. This creates a direct numerical inconsistency for the same quantity. The discrepancy likely reflects the difference between the original study's standardized β from multiple regression and the r calculated from the t-statistic, but this is never explained and the values are presented interchangeably without qualification.
issues.quote: Abstract: 'self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30).' Table 3 lists original r = -.33. Discussion: '(-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33)'

issues.description: The 95% prediction interval for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' is reported as [-.09, .26] in the Results section but as [-.07, .27] in the Discussion section. These are different intervals for the same meta-analytic result, and both bounds differ. Whether the PI includes zero is a key inferential consideration, and both versions do include zero, but reporting two different values for the same statistic undermines credibility.
issues.quote: Results: '95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065.' Discussion: 'supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.'

issues.description: The meta-analytic prediction interval for 'Opportunity to Express Self' is [.01, .14], which does not include zero. This means the meta-analytic model predicts that 95% of future studies will find a positive effect, not a null effect. Yet the authors conclude 'future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications' and 'led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect.' This is a direct misinterpretation of a PI that excludes zero—such a result supports a small positive effect, not the null hypothesis. The FSN of 3 similarly indicates the significant meta-analytic result (p = .021) is fragile, not that the null hypothesis is established.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications. The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect, but small enough to be difficult to detect.

issues.description: The Table 1 note states 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient,' but this equivalence holds only for simple linear regression with a single continuous predictor. The original Forest & Wood (2012) study reported t-statistics and degrees of freedom 'for all variables' (plural), indicating multiple regression was used, in which case β ≠ r. This is confirmed by the fact that for the Advantageous outcome, β = -.300 (Table 1) but r = -.33 (Table 3, derived from t-statistic)—a discrepancy of .03 that cannot exist if they are equivalent. The authors present the original β values and replication r values in the same column as if they are comparable, which they are not if the original used multiple regression.
issues.quote: Note. Beta coefficients are standardized (consistent with the original research). Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that one replication (Gordon College) may have summed rather than averaged items when computing subscale scores: 'the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.' If the Gordon study summed items, all of its reported means and standard deviations are incomparable to all other studies (inflated by a factor equal to the number of items per scale: 3, 3, 9, or 10 depending on subscale). While standardized betas and r values would be unaffected because standardization removes scale differences, the descriptive statistics in Table 2 for this study would be on an entirely different scale, and the scale inconsistency raises broader concerns about data quality and documentation.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: Two of the seven replication studies (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point response scale for the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, while all other studies used the original four-point scale. Additionally, IIT-Sp16 had different item wording on 4 of 10 RSE items and different item ordering. These are non-trivial deviations for a direct replication. Different response scales change the distribution of scores and potentially the construct being measured. These studies were not excluded or analyzed separately, and no formal sensitivity analysis was conducted to examine whether effect sizes differed between 4-point and 5-point scale administrations.
issues.quote: (a) one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all'), and (b) most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.description: The authors report comparing two meta-analytic estimation methods (REML and DerSimonian-Laird) and selecting REML because it 'produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data.' This is a post-hoc, results-driven model selection decision—the model was chosen based on which one yielded preferred outputs from the actual data, rather than on theoretical or pre-specified grounds. This constitutes an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom that could influence heterogeneity estimates and subsequently affect interpretation of between-study variability. No pre-registration of this choice is documented, and the DL results are not reported for comparison.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data.

issues.description: Studies varied substantially in data collection mode: three used in-lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods. One study (SAU) ran participants in groups of 2–6, violating the independence of observations assumption. These are not minor methodological variants—mode effects and social desirability pressures differ substantially between online anonymous surveys and supervised in-lab group administrations. Despite the authors acknowledging these differences, no formal test of mode as a moderator was conducted, and the studies are pooled in the meta-analysis without sensitivity analysis. The group administration at SAU particularly threatens independence assumptions underlying both the within-study regression analyses and the meta-analytic pooling.
issues.quote: As the original research did not specify whether participants completed questionnaires in a lab or online, researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods). Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.description: The fail-safe N (FSN) is a statistic designed to assess susceptibility of a significant meta-analytic result to the file-drawer problem by estimating how many null studies would be needed to render it non-significant. For 'Opportunity to Express Self,' the meta-analytic result is significant (p = .021) with FSN = 3. The authors then use this low FSN to conclude the null hypothesis is supported—an inversion of the statistic's logic. A low FSN for a significant result means that result is fragile and easily overturned, not that the null is established. The FSN is inappropriate for supporting the null hypothesis, and the method itself has been heavily criticized in the methodological literature for providing misleading reassurance in the original use case. No modern publication bias tests (e.g., Egger's test, PET-PEESE, p-curve) were conducted.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.description: The study uses cross-sectional correlational/regression methodology, measuring self-esteem and Facebook perception at the same time point. Yet the Discussion repeatedly uses predictive and quasi-causal language implying that self-esteem determines perceptions. The word 'predict' throughout is not inherently causal, but the summary statement 'we can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook' frames a correlational association as a deterministic outcome. No experimental manipulation or longitudinal design was used to establish temporal or causal ordering.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions, and that the size of this effect is considerable.

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that not all replication teams documented their procedures for handling missing data, calculating composite scores, or applying data exclusions. These decisions can substantially affect regression coefficients and effect size estimates, particularly in small samples. Without knowing whether teams used listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, mean imputation, or other approaches, the meta-analytic pooling aggregates results computed under potentially different assumptions. This limits replicability of both the individual studies and the meta-analysis itself.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc. Data were not always collected or stored consistently (e.g., race collected in some but not all studies; individual item-level data were not always stored).

issues.description: The Facebook perceptions measure was created in 2012 for the original study. The replications were conducted in 2016–2017, by which time Facebook's features, user demographics, and competitive landscape had changed substantially. The authors themselves note in the Discussion that Instagram and Snapchat had by 2016 become the preferred platforms for self-expression and social interaction among college-aged users, and that self-expression predicted usage only on Instagram and Snapchat in this cohort. This means the construct of 'perceived opportunity for self-expression on Facebook' measured in 2012 may be systematically different from the same construct measured in 2016–2017, threatening the construct equivalence that direct replication requires.
issues.quote: among Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and Snapchat, self-expression was recently found to be a significant predictor of usage only on Instagram and Snapchat among college-aged participants, and social interaction (connection in the terminology of Forest and Wood, 2012) was a greater motivation for use of Instagram and Snapchat than Facebook and Twitter.

issues.description: The Abstract states that for self-expression 'self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero).' This is accurate for the individual study CIs. However, the meta-analytic PI = [.01, .14] does not include zero, indicating the model predicts future studies will find a positive effect. The Abstract creates a misleading impression of a clean null finding by citing only the individual-study CIs while omitting the meta-analytic result (r = .08, p = .021) and the PI that excludes zero.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero)

issues.description: The Discussion claims the findings 'provide some support for social compensation theory,' yet of the four hypothesized relationships predicted by social compensation theory (lower self-esteem predicting preference for Facebook over FTF for safety, advantages, expression, and connection), only two were consistently supported (safety and, partially, advantages). The other two (expression, connection) were not supported or reversed. The authors cannot selectively cite partial support for a theory while ignoring that half the predicted effects failed to replicate, especially when the connection finding was directionally opposite to the theoretical prediction in most replications.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000; Wilson et al., 2012). This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

issues.description: The Discussion describes the safety of self-disclosure effect (meta-analytic r = -.28) as 'considerable.' By conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988), r = -.28 falls near the boundary of small-to-medium effects and would not typically be characterized as considerable without additional context. Furthermore, the sample is restricted to US undergraduates at five institutions, and only the safety and advantages effects replicated with any consistency. Describing the magnitude as 'considerable' is an interpretive overclaim that may mislead readers and practitioners about the practical significance of the finding.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions, and that the size of this effect is considerable.

issues.description: All seven replication studies used undergraduate student samples from U.S. colleges and universities, which are WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) samples. The Discussion briefly mentions Turkish students as a contrast but does not formally acknowledge that the undergraduate convenience sample limits generalizability to other age groups, educational levels, nationalities, or non-college-educated populations. The claims about how self-esteem relates to Facebook perceptions are framed broadly without this caveat being foregrounded.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.description: Table 1 notes that 'The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable' for the Express outcome, yet Table 3 reports an original r = .15 for Express. The methods state that r was calculated from t-statistics and degrees of freedom reported in the original study, but if no beta was provided for this variable, it is unclear whether a t-statistic was also provided or how r = .15 was derived. This derivation is not described anywhere in the paper, making this specific effect size non-verifiable from the information provided.
issues.quote: The original Forest and Wood (2012) regression results included t-statistics and degrees of freedom for all variables, so we chose to calculate effect size r for all four outcome variables in the study... *The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.
